title: Antikythera Mechanism
summary: The Antikythera Mechanism is a fragmentary Hellenistic astronomical machine with bronze gearwheels, made about the second century BCE. Sponge divers found a first-century BCE shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in 1900, and the mechanism was recovered from it in 1901; its 82 fragments are in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens. Its gearing could predict the movements of the Sun, Moon and planets and the timing of eclipses.

uncertainty.note: ISAW: letter forms best fit the second half of the 2nd century BCE, though a date from the end of the 3rd century to the middle of the 1st century BCE cannot be excluded. Year -99 is the midpoint of the century, not a recorded year.

as_recorded.value: made about the second century B.C.
The Greek inscriptions are carved by the same hand and date the device in the 2nd c. BC.

where.modern_name: Antikythera wreck site, east side of Antikythera island, Greece
where.historical_name: Waters off Antikythera, Aegean-Mediterranean (the wreck of a Roman-era cargo ship); the mechanism's place of manufacture is uncertain

importance.justification: The oldest known complex geared device, far beyond any other surviving ancient technology.

sources.title: The Cosmos in the Antikythera Mechanism (ISAW Papers 4)
sources.publisher: Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, New York University

sources.title: The Antikythera Mechanism, Historical Mechanical Engineering Landmark (National Archaeological Museum, Athens)

reviewer_note: Least sure of the date, which is a century-wide estimate. The pin is the wreck site (east side of Antikythera island), where it was found; the Wikidata point is the island itself, so uncertainty is 8 km. ASME says it was probably built on Rhodes but that this is not certain, so the place of manufacture is not claimed.
